extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in U.S. environmental law, EPA rulemaking, and climate policy (law students, policymakers, advocates, journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and extract the legal, scientific, and procedural criteria used to determine whether and how the EPA may regulate greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act, including endangerment findings, statutory interpretations, rulemaking procedures, advisory committee rules, and evidentiary standards. Useful for informing notice-and-comment or legal/policy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment Finding standard (Section 202(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a)(1) requires the Administrator to establish standards for motor vehicle emissions of any air pollutant which, in [her] judgment, 'cause, or contribute to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must make a scientific judgment under Section 202(a) whether greenhouse gas concentrations and emissions 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.' The 2009 action produced two distinct findings: (1) the Endangerment Finding (the mix of atmospheric concentrations of specified GHGs threatens public health and welfare); and (2) the Cause or Contribute Finding (GHG emissions from new motor vehicles contribute to atmospheric concentrations). EPA relied upon assessment reports (IPCC, U.S. Global Change Research Program, National Research Council) in reaching conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'air pollutant' and Massachusetts v. EPA precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Supreme Court in Massachusetts v. EPA held that 'greenhouse gases fit well within the Act's capacious definition of "air pollutant"' and that EPA has statutory authority to regulate GHG emissions from new motor vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal determination is a threshold statutory interpretation: if GHGs are 'air pollutants' under the CAA, EPA must consider whether to make an endangerment finding rather than declining on policy grounds. The Court also held policy judgments cannot substitute for a scientific determination about endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part Endangerment Finding (Endangerment + Cause or Contribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's 2009 determination consisted of: (1) the Endangerment Finding — specific greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6) threaten public health and welfare; and (2) the Cause or Contribute Finding — emissions from new motor vehicles and engines contribute to atmospheric concentrations and hence to the threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both elements are required to trigger vehicle emission standards under Section 202(a): evidence that the pollutants threaten health/welfare and that the source category contributes to the problem. The agency's scientific evidence (health impacts, welfare impacts like agriculture, sea-level rise, water resources, etc.) supports the endangerment conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative scientific assessment reports
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relied primarily upon assessment reports and other scientific documents produced by bodies such as the IPCC, the U.S. Global Change Research Program, and the National Research Council of the National Academy of Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking and findings are expected to be grounded in comprehensive, peer-reviewed, authoritative science. The article contrasts reliance on these broad assessments with use of a narrow/critically-reviewed report (DOE CWG) and shows that agencies are expected to consider the broader scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative rulemaking notice-and-comment and response requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the federal process required to change rules, the EPA had to consider and respond to significant public comments; inadequate responses could result in the repeal failing in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing a proposed rule opens a public comment period; the agency must consider, respond to, and legally justify its conclusions in the final rule. The EPA's proposed rescission produced hundreds of thousands of comments and the agency was required to address them; courts may invalidate rules that do not adequately respond to substantive comments or that lack adequate analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) requirements for advisory committees
rubrics_metrics.description: FACA directs that federal government advisory committees cannot form or operate in secret, that materials they create must be available to the public, and that they must have balanced membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an external working group functions as an advisory committee offering recommendations or policy advice to an agency, FACA applies: meetings and records must be public and membership must be balanced. The DOE Climate Working Group was found by a court to have violated FACA when its work provided advice rather than mere information exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial test distinguishing 'exchange of facts/information' from 'advice or recommendations' under FACA
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts examine whether a group's output constitutes mere exchange of information or whether it provides advice/recommendations to an agency; the latter triggers FACA obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailoring Rule permitting thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's Tailoring Rule limited air permitting guidelines to the largest stationary sources of GHGs, excluding smaller factories, restaurants and farms, by setting emission thresholds (e.g., permitting applied to facilities that would emit more than 100,000 tons of CO2-equivalent per year and to major modifications that would increase emissions by 75,000 tons CO2e per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailoring Rule adjusted applicability thresholds for permitting programs (New Source Review, Title V) to avoid unworkable expansion of permitting obligations to small sources. These numeric thresholds define which stationary sources are regulated for permitting purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mandatory Reporting of Greenhouse Gases Final Rule created the GHGRP that requires corporations from all sectors to report GHG emissions to EPA if above an agency-specified threshold level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting thresholds (and the GHGRP) are procedural requirements that create data and transparency about emissions; compliance depends on meeting the numeric thresholds set by EPA guidance or rule text.

rubrics_metrics.name: West Virginia v. EPA (generation-shifting limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in West Virginia v. EPA (June 2022) found that Congress did not authorize EPA to regulate 'outside the fence' options such as introducing renewable generation as a compliance mechanism under Section 111(d) (the generation-shifting approach in the Clean Power Plan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision constrains the scope of regulatory approaches available to EPA under certain CAA provisions; agencies must anchor regulatory measures within authorities clearly granted by Congress and avoid novel, large-scale systemwide strategies absent explicit congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory inclusion of specific GHGs as regulated pollutants (Inflation Reduction Act amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title VI of the Inflation Reduction Act amended the Clean Air Act to include carbon dioxide, hydrofluorocarbons, methane, nitrous oxide, perfluorocarbons, and sulfur hexafluoride as air pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative specification of pollutants clarifies the statutory basis for regulation and can strengthen the agency's authority to regulate those listed gases under the CAA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for transparent, objective, and representative scientific review
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific and professional societies (e.g., American Meteorological Society, National Academies) expect reviews used for policy to have breadth across scientific fields, reflect the full range of defensible expert views, avoid selective emphasis, and be useful for informed policy and decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports relied upon in rulemaking should be methodologically sound, transparently produced, and subject to appropriate peer review; criticisms of the DOE CWG report included cherry-picking, misrepresentation, and lack of representative expertise — all factors that undermine reliance on such reports for regulatory justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of economic analysis and cost-benefit reasoning in justification of regulation or deregulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA's proposed rescission argued that harm caused by regulating vehicle emissions exceeded benefits; agencies commonly present economic and engineering analyses to justify regulation or deregulatory actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory actions frequently depend on economic assessments of costs and benefits; however, legal challenges may focus on whether the agency's economic analysis appropriately addressed scientific evidence, uncertainties, and statutory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider 'most recently available science' and scientific consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are expected to consider the most recently available science when making findings and to explain their scientific basis. The EPA said it considered IPCC Sixth Assessment Report and other sources but relied extensively on the DOE CWG draft report in its proposed rescission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency cannot ignore or selectively discount the broader scientific consensus without adequate explanation; courts and scientific bodies may scrutinize departures from consensus and the adequacy of the agency's evidentiary basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment period timing and procedural posting requirements (Federal Register, OIRA review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rules are submitted for interagency review (e.g., OIRA), published in the Federal Register, and opened for public comment for defined periods; meetings with stakeholders (lobbyists, industry, advocates) are recorded in the regulatory process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administrative record must show appropriate interagency review and public notice. Short or inadequate comment periods, or failures in interagency review, can be grounds for legal challenge. The EPA's rescission proposed rule had specified comment periods (later extended) and underwent OIRA/White House processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible evidence of endangerment: health and welfare impacts list
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA articulated specific categories of ways GHGs may endanger public health (heat-related mortality, degraded air quality/ground-level ozone, extreme weather effects, expansion of climate-sensitive diseases) and public welfare (agriculture, forestry, water resources, sea level rise, energy impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated impacts constitute the substance of the scientific showing the agency uses to satisfy the 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger' standard; a robust administrative record links pollutant concentrations to these concrete harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Act and peer review expectations for agency-used reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and experts insisted DOE's CWG report be subjected to unbiased, robust, and transparent peer review under the Information Quality Act and other federal requirements before being relied upon by an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies relying on externally produced reports for rulemaking should ensure the reports meet information quality and peer-review standards; failing to do so invites legal challenge and criticism of the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority limits and statutory textualism in agency interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA (in its rescission proposal) advanced a narrow reading of the Clean Air Act, arguing that Congress did not authorize certain greenhouse gas regulations; legal attacks and defenses pivot on statutory text and precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory scope depends on statutory interpretation and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Massachusetts, West Virginia). Agencies must ground their interpretations in textual and precedential support; novel readings risk judicial reversal.
